title: UAE Corporate Tax 2024: The Complete Guide for Businesses
excerpt: Everything businesses need to know about UAE Corporate Tax — who pays, what qualifies, free zone treatment, and how to stay compliant with the 9% regime effective from June 2023.
content:
Introduction: UAE Corporate Tax is Now a Reality

The UAE Federal Corporate Tax (CT) regime — effective for financial years starting on or after 1 June 2023 — represents the most significant shift in UAE tax policy in a generation. With a headline rate of 9% on taxable income above AED 375,000, businesses across every emirate must now understand their obligations or risk material penalties.

This guide covers who is subject to Corporate Tax, what income qualifies for the 0% Free Zone rate, key exemptions, and how to structure your compliance process.

Who Is Subject to UAE Corporate Tax?

Corporate Tax applies to all juridical persons incorporated in the UAE, including mainland companies, free zone entities, branches of foreign companies, and — in limited circumstances — natural persons conducting business in the UAE. Individuals earning salary, investment income, or rental income from personally held property are generally outside scope.

  • Mainland companies: Subject to 9% CT on taxable income above AED 375,000.
  • Free Zone entities: Subject to CT but may qualify for a 0% rate on "Qualifying Income" if they meet specific conditions.
  • Foreign companies: Taxable if they have a Permanent Establishment (PE) in the UAE or earn UAE-sourced income.

The AED 375,000 Threshold and Small Business Relief

Taxable income up to AED 375,000 is taxed at 0%. Income above this threshold is taxed at 9%. In addition, businesses with revenue below AED 3,000,000 may elect for "Small Business Relief" and be treated as having no taxable income for a given tax period — a significant concession for startups and SMEs.

Free Zone Qualifying Income: The Critical Rules

Free Zone Persons (FZPs) can benefit from a 0% Qualifying Free Zone Person (QFZP) rate on their Qualifying Income, provided they:

  1. Maintain adequate substance in the UAE;
  2. Derive Qualifying Income (income from transactions with other Free Zone Persons or from Qualifying Activities with non-Free Zone persons);
  3. Comply with transfer pricing requirements;
  4. Have not elected to be subject to the standard CT regime.

Qualifying Activities include manufacturing, processing, holding shares and other securities, treasury and financing services, distribution within a designated zone, and more. Non-Qualifying Income (e.g., income from UAE mainland customers for certain activities) will be taxed at 9%.

Key Exemptions and Reliefs

The UAE CT regime includes several important exemptions:

  • Participation Exemption: Dividends and capital gains from qualifying shareholdings (≥5% ownership, held ≥12 months) are exempt.
  • Foreign PE Exemption: Profits attributable to a foreign PE can be exempt if the foreign jurisdiction taxes them.
  • Government entities and extractive businesses are broadly exempt from CT.
  • Interest Deduction Limitation: Net interest expense is capped at 30% of EBITDA (with a safe harbour of AED 12 million).

Transfer Pricing and Related-Party Transactions

The UAE CT law codifies the arm's length principle. All transactions between related parties must be priced as if conducted between independent parties. Businesses are required to maintain contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation — a Transfer Pricing Disclosure Form must be filed with the CT return.

Registration, Filing, and Payment Deadlines

All taxable persons must register with the Federal Tax Authority (FTA) and obtain a Tax Registration Number (TRN). The CT return must be filed and tax paid within 9 months of the end of the tax period. Penalties for late registration and filing can be significant.

Early engagement is always more cost-effective than reactive compliance. Contact us for a confidential assessment.
author: Marwan Negm

title: Free Zone vs Mainland Company in UAE: Which Is Right for Your Business?
excerpt: A practical comparison of Free Zone and Mainland company formation in the UAE — covering ownership, visas, office requirements, trade restrictions, and the 2024 Corporate Tax implications.
content:
The Most Important Business Decision You Will Make in the UAE

One of the first and most consequential decisions any entrepreneur faces when entering the UAE market is whether to establish a Free Zone company or a Mainland (onshore) company. The wrong choice can cost you years of restructuring. The right choice sets a profitable, compliant foundation.

In 2024, the decision is more nuanced than ever — particularly following the introduction of UAE Corporate Tax and the removal of the 49%/51% foreign ownership restriction on mainland companies.

What is a UAE Free Zone Company?

The UAE has over 40 free zones, each designed to attract specific industries: DIFC and ADGM for financial services, JAFZA for logistics and trading, Dubai Media City for creative industries, and dozens more. Free Zone companies benefit from:

  • 100% foreign ownership (always available in free zones)
  • Potential 0% Corporate Tax on Qualifying Income (see our CT guide)
  • Full repatriation of profits and capital
  • Simplified company formation processes
  • Sector-specific infrastructure and networking

The key limitation: a pure Free Zone entity cannot directly conduct business with UAE mainland customers without appointing a mainland distributor or establishing a mainland branch — which adds cost and complexity.

What is a UAE Mainland Company?

A mainland company is licensed by the Department of Economic Development (DED) of the relevant emirate. The game-changer since 2021: most business activities are now open to 100% foreign ownership on the mainland — removing the historic requirement for a 51% UAE national shareholder for most sectors.

Mainland companies can:

  • Trade freely with UAE government entities and mainland businesses
  • Bid on government contracts without restriction
  • Open offices in any location across the UAE
  • Engage in a wider range of activities

The trade-off: mainland companies pay 9% Corporate Tax on profits above AED 375,000 (no 0% Free Zone treatment) and face slightly more administrative requirements.

Visa Quotas: A Practical Consideration

Free Zone visa allocations are typically tied to office space. A "flexi-desk" or virtual office in a free zone usually provides 1-3 visa quotas. Mainland companies generally offer more flexibility in visa issuance, particularly for labour-intensive businesses.

The 2024 Corporate Tax Factor

Post-Corporate Tax, the Free Zone 0% rate remains attractive — but only for genuinely qualifying businesses. If a significant portion of your revenue comes from mainland UAE customers, a Free Zone structure may be inefficient. A dual structure (Free Zone holding company + mainland operating subsidiary) can work but adds complexity and compliance cost.

Our Recommendation Framework

Choose a Free Zone if: your target market is international, you need the 0% CT benefit, your activity qualifies, and direct mainland trade is not critical.

Choose Mainland if: you intend to trade primarily with UAE entities, you need a physical retail presence, you are bidding on government contracts, or you want maximum flexibility.

Consider a dual structure if: you have both international and mainland activities at significant scale.

Nexus Axis Consultants provides end-to-end business setup advisory — from activity selection and jurisdiction analysis to licensing, visa processing, and bank account opening. Contact us to build the right structure from day one.
author: Layla Al Rashidi

title: DIFC Courts Explained: Jurisdiction, Process, and When to Use Them
excerpt: A comprehensive guide to the DIFC Courts — their jurisdiction, how proceedings work, enforcement of judgments, and why many businesses choose DIFC over onshore UAE courts for commercial disputes.
content:
What Are the DIFC Courts?

The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) Courts are a sophisticated, independent common law judiciary operating within the DIFC free zone. Established in 2004 and modelled on the best common law courts internationally, the DIFC Courts adjudicate in English under a system that any international business will recognise: precedent-based, procedurally transparent, and with judgments that can be readily enforced both in the UAE and internationally.

For international businesses operating in or doing business with the UAE, the DIFC Courts frequently represent the preferred forum for commercial dispute resolution.

DIFC Court Jurisdiction: Who Can Use Them?

The DIFC Courts have jurisdiction over:

  • Disputes arising from transactions, agreements, or matters connected to the DIFC;
  • Cases where parties have contractually agreed to DIFC Court jurisdiction — even if neither party is DIFC-based (the "opt-in" jurisdiction under Practice Direction No. 1 of 2014);
  • Civil and commercial matters where the claim value exceeds USD 100,000 (Small Claims Tribunal for lower-value claims);
  • Employment disputes between employers and employees within the DIFC.

The "opt-in" jurisdiction is particularly powerful: two parties anywhere in the world can choose DIFC Courts as their forum simply by including a DIFC Courts jurisdiction clause in their contract.

The Small Claims Tribunal (SCT)

For claims up to USD 200,000, the DIFC Small Claims Tribunal provides a fast-track process — hearings are often completed within weeks, costs are lower, and legal representation is not required (though it is advisable).

How DIFC Court Proceedings Work

Proceedings in the Court of First Instance follow a well-structured timetable:

  1. Claim filed and served on the defendant;
  2. Defence and Counterclaim (if any) filed within 28 days;
  3. Case Management Conference (CMC) — the judge sets the timetable for disclosure, witness statements, and expert evidence;
  4. Trial — conducted in English, with oral evidence from witnesses and cross-examination;
  5. Judgment — written, reasoned, and publicly available.

Enforcement of DIFC Court Judgments

A DIFC Court judgment can be enforced directly against assets located in the DIFC. For enforcement across the wider UAE (onshore Dubai, Abu Dhabi, etc.), a DIFC judgment is recognised and enforced through a streamlined process via the UAE onshore courts — a significant practical advantage over foreign court judgments, which face a more arduous recognition process.

Internationally, DIFC judgments have been recognised in the UK, Singapore, and other common law jurisdictions.

DIFC Courts vs. Onshore UAE Courts: The Key Differences

FactorDIFC CourtsOnshore UAE Courts
LanguageEnglishArabic
Legal systemCommon lawCivil law (UAE Federal Law)
PrecedentYes — published judgmentsLimited
SpeedGenerally fasterVariable
International enforcementStrongRequires recognition process

When Should You Use the DIFC Courts?

Consider DIFC Courts when: your counterparty is an international business; the contract value is substantial; you want an English-language, common law process; or your contract was negotiated in English under international commercial norms.

Our litigation team at Nexus Axis Consultants has extensive experience in DIFC Court proceedings — from interim injunctions and freezing orders to full trial and enforcement. We advise clients on drafting effective DIFC jurisdiction clauses before disputes arise, and represent them with full vigour when they do.

title: How to Set Up a Company in Dubai in 2024: Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: A practical, step-by-step guide to company formation in Dubai in 2024 — covering mainland and free zone options, required documents, timelines, costs, visa quotas, and bank account opening.
content:
Why Dubai Remains the Gateway to MENA Business

Dubai continues to rank among the world's top destinations for business formation. Its strategic location, world-class infrastructure, zero personal income tax, and the UAE's bilateral investment treaty network make it an unrivalled hub for entrepreneurs and multinationals alike. In 2024, with 100% foreign ownership available across most mainland activities and over 40 free zones to choose from, the opportunity has never been more accessible.

This guide walks you through the key steps — whether you are setting up a Dubai mainland company or a free zone entity.

Step 1: Choose Your Business Activity

The UAE's licensing system is activity-based. Every company must specify its licensed activities, and the choice of activity determines which jurisdictions and license types are available to you. Common categories include:

  • Commercial (trading, import/export, retail)
  • Professional (consulting, legal, accounting, IT services)
  • Industrial (manufacturing, processing)
  • Tourism and hospitality

Choosing the wrong activity category is a common mistake that creates compliance problems later. Legal advice at this stage saves significant cost.

Step 2: Select Your Jurisdiction

As detailed in our Free Zone vs Mainland guide, the jurisdiction choice fundamentally shapes your company's capabilities and tax treatment. Key questions to answer:

  • Do you need to trade directly with UAE mainland customers?
  • Are you eligible for Free Zone Qualifying Income (0% CT)?
  • What are your visa requirements?
  • Do you need a physical office, warehouse, or can you operate remotely?

Step 3: Reserve Your Trade Name

Your company name must comply with UAE naming regulations: no offensive terms, no names of existing entities, and for mainland companies, no abbreviations of country names. Names can be reserved online via the DED portal (mainland) or the relevant free zone authority.

Step 4: Prepare and Notarise Documents

Typical documentation requirements include:

  • Passport copies of all shareholders and directors
  • Memorandum and Articles of Association (notarised)
  • Board resolution and power of attorney (for corporate shareholders)
  • Proof of address for all principals
  • Business plan (required by some free zones and banks)

Foreign documents typically require apostille certification and legalisation at the UAE Embassy in the country of origin.

Step 5: Secure Your Office Space

A registered office address is mandatory. Options range from a virtual or flexi-desk (free zones) to a dedicated physical office. The office Ejari (tenancy registration) is required for both the trade license and visa applications.

Step 6: Obtain Your Trade License

Mainland licenses are issued by the Dubai DED; free zone licenses by the relevant free zone authority. Processing times range from 1-5 working days for simple structures to several weeks for regulated activities (financial services, legal, healthcare). Government fees typically range from AED 10,000–25,000 depending on activity and structure.

Step 7: Apply for Visas

Once the trade license is issued, you can apply for UAE residence visas for shareholders, managers, and employees. The process involves: entry permit, medical examination, Emirates ID application, and visa stamping. Total processing time is typically 2-4 weeks.

Step 8: Open a Corporate Bank Account

Bank account opening in the UAE has become more thorough due to anti-money laundering requirements. Expect extensive KYC documentation, a business plan, financial projections, and in many cases an in-person interview. Processing time can range from 4-12 weeks depending on the bank and business nature. We strongly recommend engaging a legal advisor to prepare a compelling bank introduction package.

Nexus Axis Business Setup Services

Our business setup team has successfully incorporated over 200 entities across UAE jurisdictions in the past five years. We manage the entire process — from activity selection and jurisdiction analysis to license issuance, visa processing, and bank account opening — typically completing straightforward structures within 15-25 business days. Contact us to begin.

title: UAE Labour Law 2022 (Federal Decree-Law No. 33): What Employers and Employees Must Know
excerpt: A practical guide to UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 (effective February 2022) — covering new contract types, termination rules, end-of-service gratuity, non-compete clauses, and MOHRE dispute resolution.
content:
The 2022 UAE Labour Law Revolution

Federal Decree-Law No. 33 of 2021 — which replaced the UAE Labour Law of 1980 entirely — came into effect on 2 February 2022. It introduced the most comprehensive overhaul of UAE employment law in four decades. Every employer in the UAE (outside financial free zones with their own employment regulations) must be compliant. Failure to comply creates significant legal and financial exposure.

New Contract Types

The landmark change: unlimited-term contracts are abolished. All employment contracts must now be fixed-term, with a maximum duration of 3 years (renewable). Employees on existing unlimited-term contracts were required to transition to fixed-term contracts by February 2023.

The law also introduces five new work patterns beyond the traditional full-time model:

  • Part-time employment
  • Temporary employment
  • Flexible working
  • Remote/telework
  • Job-sharing arrangements

Termination: Grounds, Notice, and Protections

An employer may terminate an employee for legitimate reasons. The law prohibits termination for reasons related to gender, race, colour, religion, national origin, social origin, or disability. Protected categories are broader than before.

Notice periods:

  • Minimum 30 days notice required in all cases where either party terminates
  • Maximum notice period: 90 days

Arbitrary dismissal (termination without legitimate cause) entitles the employee to compensation of up to 3 months' remuneration in addition to other entitlements.

End-of-Service Gratuity: The Calculation

Gratuity entitlement continues under the new law, accruing at:

  • 21 days' basic salary per year for the first 5 years of service
  • 30 days' basic salary per year for each subsequent year

Gratuity is calculated on basic salary only (excluding allowances) and is payable upon termination regardless of which party initiated it — except in cases of employee misconduct as specified in the law. An important change: gratuity is no longer forfeited for employees who resign before completing 1 year of service.

Non-Compete Clauses

The new law clarifies the enforceability of non-compete restrictions: they are valid if limited in terms of time (maximum 2 years), geography, and the nature of activities restricted. Courts will scrutinise overly broad non-compete clauses closely. Employers must pay consideration for the restriction to be robust.

Anti-Discrimination and Harassment

For the first time, UAE law explicitly prohibits workplace bullying and harassment and includes provisions for equal pay between men and women for equivalent work. The Ministerial Decree implementing these provisions requires employers to have written anti-harassment policies.

MOHRE Dispute Resolution

Employment disputes must first be referred to the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation (MOHRE) for conciliation. If unresolved within 2 weeks, MOHRE refers the matter to the Labour Courts. Critically, filing a MOHRE complaint triggers an automatic freeze on the employer's ability to recruit new staff — a powerful lever for employees.

How We Help

author: Sara Al Hamdan

title: International Arbitration in the UAE: DIAC, ICC, and Choosing the Right Forum
excerpt: A guide for businesses on international arbitration in the UAE — comparing DIAC, ICC, and LCIA rules; drafting effective arbitration clauses; enforcement under the New York Convention; and interim relief options.
content:
Why International Arbitration Matters for UAE Businesses

International arbitration is the preferred mechanism for resolving cross-border commercial disputes for a compelling reason: unlike court judgments, arbitral awards are enforceable in over 170 countries under the 1958 New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, to which the UAE acceded in 2006.

For businesses contracting across borders — as most UAE businesses do — an arbitration clause is not optional; it is essential commercial protection.

UAE Arbitration Law: Federal Arbitration Law No. 6 of 2018

The UAE Federal Arbitration Law, modelled on the UNCITRAL Model Law, governs arbitrations seated in the UAE (excluding the DIFC and ADGM, which have their own arbitration laws). It provides a modern framework: courts intervene minimally, awards are confidential, and enforcement procedures are streamlined.

The Dubai International Arbitration Centre (DIAC)

DIAC is the UAE's primary arbitration institution, reconstituted under a new statute in 2022. Key features of the 2022 DIAC Rules:

  • Expedited procedure for claims under USD 2 million
  • Emergency arbitrator mechanism for urgent interim relief
  • Robust provisions for multi-party and multi-contract disputes
  • Transparent fee schedule based on claim value

DIAC is the natural choice for disputes with a UAE nexus: fast, cost-effective, and with a growing body of institutional experience.

ICC Arbitration from the UAE

The International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) is the world's most prestigious arbitration institution. ICC arbitration from a UAE seat offers the full weight of ICC's institutional infrastructure, global neutrality, and its Terms of Reference process. It is preferred by sophisticated international counterparties and financial institutions.

ICC is typically more expensive than DIAC but provides unparalleled credibility for high-value, complex multi-jurisdictional disputes.

DIFC-LCIA: The Specialist Financial Centre Option

For disputes involving DIFC entities or contracts expressly choosing DIFC law, the DIFC-LCIA (now the DIFC Arbitration Centre following LCIA's withdrawal) offers common law-aligned arbitration within the DIFC's independent legal system.

Drafting an Effective Arbitration Clause

A defective arbitration clause is one of the most expensive drafting mistakes a business can make. A valid, enforceable clause must specify:

  1. The arbitration institution (e.g., DIAC, ICC);
  2. The seat of arbitration (e.g., "Dubai, UAE");
  3. The number of arbitrators (1 for smaller disputes, 3 for complex);
  4. The language of the proceedings;
  5. The governing law of the main contract.

Pathological clauses — those with ambiguities about the institution or seat — can result in years of jurisdictional litigation before the merits are even reached.

Interim Relief: Freezing Orders and Emergency Arbitrators

A common concern: can I freeze assets while arbitration proceeds? Yes. Both the UAE courts (under Article 21 of the Arbitration Law) and, for DIAC and ICC proceedings, the emergency arbitrator mechanism can provide urgent interim relief including asset freezing orders, injunctions, and production of evidence.

Nexus Axis Consultants has secured precautionary attachments in the UAE courts within 72 hours of filing in multiple matters. Speed is critical: assets dissipated before a freezing order are rarely recovered.

Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards in the UAE

The UAE's accession to the New York Convention means foreign awards are enforceable. The practical process: file the award and arbitration agreement (with certified Arabic translation) in the Court of First Instance of the relevant emirate. UAE courts have shown increasing deference to foreign awards, particularly from established institutions.
author: Mohab Samy

title: Off-Plan Property Disputes in UAE: Your Legal Rights as a Buyer
excerpt: What to do when a UAE off-plan developer delays, cancels, or fails to deliver your property. A guide to RERA complaints, SPA remedies, deposit recovery, and taking legal action against developers.
content:
The Off-Plan Property Market in the UAE

The UAE — and Dubai in particular — has one of the world's most active off-plan property markets. Millions of dirhams are invested annually in properties sold before construction is complete. When developers perform, buyers receive capital appreciation and a quality asset. When developers fail — and some do — buyers face a complex legal landscape that requires expert navigation.

This guide explains your rights and the remedies available to you as a purchaser of off-plan property in the UAE.

The Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA): Your Primary Instrument

Your SPA is the foundation of your legal rights. It should specify:

  • The promised handover date;
  • The unit specifications and plot area;
  • The payment schedule and total purchase price;
  • Termination rights and refund provisions for both parties;
  • Liquidated damages for delay (if any).

Many SPAs are drafted by developers and are heavily weighted in their favour. Having a lawyer review your SPA before signing is always advisable.

RERA: The Regulator for Dubai Off-Plan Disputes

The Real Estate Regulatory Agency (RERA), a division of the Dubai Land Department (DLD), regulates off-plan sales in Dubai. Developers must register projects and escrow accounts with RERA before accepting deposits. Key protections:

  • Deposits must be held in a registered escrow account — not accessible to the developer except against certified construction milestones;
  • RERA publishes project completion percentages, allowing buyers to verify progress;
  • The Oqood system registers all off-plan contracts, providing a legal record of your purchase.

Developer Delays: Your Options

If your developer has missed the handover date:

  1. Check your SPA: Does it contain a grace period (typically 12 months post-agreed handover) before termination rights arise?
  2. File a RERA complaint: RERA can compel the developer to update buyers on the project status and timeline.
  3. Demand compensation: If your SPA includes liquidated damages for delay, you can claim them. If not, common law damages for delay may be available.
  4. Consider termination: In extreme cases (developer has failed to progress, project is cancelled, insolvency), you may have a right to terminate and recover your deposit.

The Rental Disputes Centre and Dubai Courts

For disputes not resolved through RERA's conciliation mechanism, the Dubai Courts handle off-plan property litigation. Our real estate team has successfully recovered 100% deposits plus statutory compensation for clients whose developers failed to deliver within contracted periods.

Cancelled Projects: Recovering Your Deposit

If RERA formally cancels a project, the developer must refund all payments from the escrow account. In practice, escrow funds are sometimes insufficient (particularly where developers have drawn down against construction milestones). In these cases, claims against the developer's other assets — and in some cases, its directors personally — may be available.

We advise clients to act quickly: asset dissipation by distressed developers is a real risk. A precautionary attachment obtained early can make the difference between full recovery and a hollow judgment.

Abu Dhabi Off-Plan: ADRD and the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department

Abu Dhabi off-plan transactions are regulated by the Abu Dhabi Department of Municipalities and Transport (DMT). The Abu Dhabi Real Estate Dispute Resolution Centre (ADRD) handles disputes. The framework is broadly similar to Dubai's RERA regime but with some procedural differences.
author: Khaled Mansour

title: Emiratisation (Nafis) in 2024: What Every UAE Employer Must Know
excerpt: A practical guide to UAE Emiratisation obligations for private sector employers in 2024 — covering Nafis quotas, MOHRE penalties, the Targeted Emiratisation programme, and how to build a compliant workforce strategy.
content:
Emiratisation: A National Priority with Real Legal Consequences

Emiratisation — the UAE government's policy to increase UAE nationals' participation in the private sector workforce — is no longer a soft aspiration. The Targeted Emiratisation programme, backed by Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2023, imposes mandatory quotas with significant financial penalties for non-compliance. For employers with 50 or more employees, this is now one of the most consequential compliance obligations in the UAE.

Who Is Subject to Emiratisation Requirements?

The current mandatory Emiratisation targets apply to private sector establishments with 50 or more employees. The targets are sector-specific and are set by MOHRE. From 2024, companies in 14 targeted sectors must achieve:

  • 2% annual increase in Emirati employees for companies with 50-499 employees;
  • Higher percentage targets for companies in financial services, insurance, and other priority sectors.

The Nafis programme (run by the Emirati Talent Competitiveness Council) subsidises Emirati salaries, reducing the cost differential for employers who proactively hire UAE nationals.

Financial Penalties for Non-Compliance

The penalties for failing to meet Emiratisation targets are not theoretical — they are enforced. Non-compliant employers face:

  • AED 96,000 per year per Emirati employee shortfall (i.e., AED 8,000 per month per unfilled quota position);
  • Suspension of the ability to obtain new work permits for non-UAE national employees;
  • In persistent cases, restrictions on business license renewal.

These penalties compound rapidly for companies with multiple unfilled quota positions.

The Nafis Subsidy: Making Emiratisation Commercially Viable

The Nafis salary support scheme subsidises Emirati employees' salaries in private sector roles, covering a portion of the salary cost for a defined period. For roles paying AED 3,000–20,000 per month, Nafis can cover up to 30% of the salary during the support period, significantly narrowing the cost gap between Emirati and expatriate hires.

Employers who engage proactively with Nafis and document their Emiratisation efforts in good faith are better positioned in the event of a MOHRE inspection.

Practical Compliance Steps for Employers

  1. Calculate your current Emiratisation rate using your Wages Protection System (WPS) data and MOHRE portal;
  2. Identify your sector-specific targets and project the shortfall;
  3. Develop a hiring plan — work with Nafis and university career offices to build a pipeline;
  4. Review job descriptions to ensure they are accessible to UAE nationals;
  5. Engage with Nafis to register for salary support;
  6. Document all Emiratisation efforts — MOHRE gives weight to demonstrated good faith.

Emiratisation in Financial Free Zones (DIFC and ADGM)

DIFC and ADGM have their own Emiratisation frameworks, implemented through their respective regulators. The targets and penalty structures differ from the MOHRE regime. If you employ staff in both onshore UAE and DIFC/ADGM, you must comply with both frameworks simultaneously.

title: Precautionary Attachment in UAE: How to Freeze Assets Before Judgment
excerpt: A practical guide to UAE precautionary attachment orders — who can apply, the legal grounds required, how quickly courts act, and strategic considerations for creditors seeking to protect their claims before assets disappear.
content:
When a Claim Is Not Enough: The Need for Precautionary Attachment

Winning a judgment is only valuable if there are assets against which to enforce it. In commercial disputes — particularly those involving potential fraud, asset dissipation, or a counterparty that may move assets offshore — securing a precautionary attachment (hajz tah affuzi) before or immediately after filing a claim is often more important than the claim itself.

UAE law provides one of the most powerful and responsive precautionary attachment regimes in the MENA region. Our team has obtained attachments within 72 hours in multiple matters.

Legal Basis: UAE Civil Procedure Code

Precautionary attachment is governed by Articles 252-262 of the UAE Civil Procedure Code (Federal Law No. 42 of 2022, replacing the 1992 code). A claimant may apply to the court to attach the debtor's assets — whether movable or immovable — including bank accounts, real estate, vehicles, shares, and receivables.

The Legal Requirements for Obtaining Attachment

The court will grant a precautionary attachment if the applicant demonstrates:

  1. A prima facie claim: A credible basis for the underlying claim (contract, cheque, judgment debt, etc.);
  2. A risk of dissipation: Evidence or reasonable grounds to believe the debtor may transfer, conceal, or dissipate assets to frustrate enforcement.

The application is made ex parte (without notice to the debtor) and decided by a judge, often on the same day or within 24-48 hours of filing.

What Assets Can Be Attached?

Virtually all assets of the debtor can be attached:

  • Bank accounts (in any UAE bank) — a bank garnishment order freezes all accounts;
  • Real property registered with the relevant land department;
  • Vehicles, marine vessels, and aircraft;
  • Shares in UAE companies;
  • Receivables owed by third parties to the debtor.

The Risk of a "Bounced" Attachment

If the court later finds the underlying claim is meritless or the attachment was obtained without proper grounds, the applicant may be liable to compensate the debtor for damages caused by the wrongful attachment. This is why precise, well-documented applications are essential.

Post-Attachment: The Follow-Up Claim

A precautionary attachment is a preservation measure — it does not determine the merits of the dispute. The claimant must file the substantive claim before the competent court within the period set by the attachment order (typically 8 days from the attachment date). Failure to file within this period causes the attachment to lapse automatically.

DIFC and ADGM Courts: Freezing Injunctions

For disputes within the DIFC and ADGM jurisdictions, the equivalent mechanism is a freezing injunction (known internationally as a Mareva injunction). DIFC and ADGM Courts can also grant worldwide freezing injunctions in appropriate cases — a powerful tool against respondents with assets in multiple jurisdictions.

Strategic Considerations

Speed and discretion are paramount. A debtor who becomes aware of an impending attachment application will often move assets immediately. Our litigation team is experienced in preparing attachment applications swiftly, without alerting counterparties, and managing the entire process from court filing to bank notification — often within a single business day.
author: Marwan Negm

title: UAE Golden Visa: Legal Requirements, Eligibility, and How to Apply in 2024
excerpt: Everything you need to know about the UAE Golden Visa in 2024 — who qualifies (investors, professionals, entrepreneurs, students), the application process, benefits, and how a legal advisor can help secure your long-term residency.
content:
What is the UAE Golden Visa?

The UAE Golden Visa is a long-term residency programme introduced in 2019 and significantly expanded in 2022, granting qualifying individuals 10-year renewable residency in the UAE without the need for a national sponsor. It represents one of the most attractive long-term residency programmes in the world — combining the UAE's zero personal income tax environment with unparalleled global mobility.

As of 2024, over 150,000 Golden Visas have been issued, with the programme actively expanding its eligible categories.

Who Qualifies for the UAE Golden Visa?

Investors

  • Real estate investors with property valued at AED 2 million or more (including mortgaged property, provided equity of AED 2M is confirmed by a bank letter);
  • Investors with a public investment of AED 2 million or more in UAE funds, companies, or as a registered business owner with AED 2M capital;
  • Shareholders with UAE company deposits of AED 2M+.

Entrepreneurs

  • Owners of a UAE startup assessed at AED 500,000+ by an approved business incubator;
  • Entrepreneurs with a previous successful exit of AED 1M+ from a UAE project.

Professionals

  • Specialists in science, engineering, healthcare, education, business, and culture;
  • Professionals with a monthly salary of AED 30,000+ in a specified priority field and holding a Bachelor's degree;
  • UAE licensed doctors, engineers, scientists, and artists recognised by relevant authorities.

Students and Graduates

  • Secondary school students with a GPA of 95%+ from UAE or accredited international schools;
  • University graduates with a GPA of 3.75+ from top-ranked global universities.

Humanitarian Pioneers and Creative Talents

  • Individuals nominated by ICA and relevant federal entities for exceptional contributions.

Benefits of the UAE Golden Visa

  • 10-year residency, renewable;
  • No requirement for a UAE national sponsor;
  • Ability to live outside the UAE for more than 6 months without the visa lapsing;
  • Sponsor immediate family members (spouse, children, and domestic workers);
  • Full access to UAE banking, business, and educational services;
  • Multiple entry visa during the application process.

The Application Process

  1. Pre-approval: Determine eligibility category and gather supporting documentation;
  2. Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs and Ports Security (ICA) application (via smart.ica.gov.ae) or through the relevant emirate's immigration office;
  3. Medical examination and biometrics;
  4. Emirates ID issuance;
  5. Visa stamping in passport.

Total processing time is typically 4-8 weeks from a complete application submission.

Common Pitfalls

Incorrect category selection, missing documentation, and failure to provide valuation letters in the correct format are the most common causes of delay or rejection. Given the stakes — a 10-year residency — professional assistance pays for itself many times over.

title: How to Resolve a Commercial Dispute in the UAE: Courts, MOHRE, and Alternative Dispute Resolution
excerpt: A practical roadmap for UAE businesses facing commercial disputes — comparing UAE onshore courts, DIFC Courts, DIAC arbitration, and mediation, with strategic advice on choosing the right path and preserving evidence.
content:
Facing a Commercial Dispute in the UAE: Your Options

A commercial dispute in the UAE can arise without warning — a defaulting buyer, a supplier who fails to deliver, a partner who diverts company funds, or a landlord who wrongfully terminates your lease. The UAE offers multiple dispute resolution pathways, and choosing the right one at the outset can mean the difference between a swift resolution and years of costly litigation.

Step One: Preserve Your Evidence

Before any formal step, secure your evidence. In the UAE (as in most jurisdictions), documents destroyed or lost after a dispute arises cannot be recreated. Immediately:

  • Preserve all contracts, emails, WhatsApp messages, invoices, and bank records;
  • Obtain certified bank statements showing payment flows;
  • Secure witness statements from employees while recollections are fresh;
  • If digital evidence may be altered, consider notarised screen captures or third-party forensic preservation.

UAE Onshore Courts: The Default Forum

UAE onshore civil and commercial courts operate in Arabic under a civil law system. They are the default forum for most commercial disputes not subject to a contractual arbitration or DIFC clause. Key features:

  • Written submissions — oral argument plays a lesser role than in common law courts;
  • Judges rather than juries decide fact and law;
  • Court-appointed experts are commonly used for technical or financial disputes;
  • Appeals as of right to the Court of Appeal and (on points of law) to the Court of Cassation.

Timelines vary by emirate and court complexity — simple claims can resolve in 6-18 months; complex multi-party litigation may take 2-4 years through all appeal stages.

Urgent Relief: Precautionary Attachments and Injunctions

If your counterparty may dissipate assets or take damaging action before a hearing, apply immediately for a precautionary attachment or injunction. These ex parte applications can be decided within 24-72 hours and immediately freeze the respondent's bank accounts and property.

Demand Letters and Pre-Litigation Strategy

A well-drafted demand letter from a law firm frequently resolves disputes without litigation. It signals seriousness, creates a paper trail of the creditor's attempts to resolve the matter, and — in some circumstances — triggers contractual dispute resolution procedures that must be exhausted before proceedings can commence.

DIAC Arbitration: Speed and Confidentiality

If your contract contains an arbitration clause, the dispute must go to arbitration. Even where there is no clause, parties can mutually agree to arbitrate. DIAC's 2022 Rules provide an expedited track for claims under USD 2 million, with a target final award within 6 months. Arbitration offers a key advantage over litigation: confidentiality — proceedings and awards are not public.

Mediation: The Often-Overlooked Option

UAE courts increasingly encourage mediation at the outset of proceedings — the Abu Dhabi and Dubai courts both operate mediation centres. For commercial disputes where the parties have an ongoing relationship (long-term supplier, landlord, joint venture partner), mediation can achieve a commercially sensible resolution in days rather than years, at a fraction of the litigation cost.

Choosing the Right Path: Our Framework

  • Contract has arbitration clause → arbitration (check institution and seat carefully);
  • Contract has DIFC clause → DIFC Courts;
  • Assets at risk of dissipation → precautionary attachment first, then substantive claim;
  • Ongoing relationship → mediation or conciliation first;
  • All else → UAE onshore courts.

Our litigation team evaluates every dispute on its specific facts and recommends the forum most likely to achieve the best outcome at the lowest proportionate cost. Contact us for a confidential case assessment — ideally before you send your first demand letter.

title: Corporate Tax Free Zone Qualifying Income in UAE: The Definitive 2024 Guide
excerpt: A deep-dive into UAE Corporate Tax Qualifying Free Zone Person status — what income qualifies, which activities count, the substance requirements, and how to structure your free zone business to legitimately access the 0% CT rate.
content:
The 0% Free Zone Rate: Valuable But Conditional

The UAE Corporate Tax law preserves the historic 0% tax rate for free zone businesses — but only for those that qualify. A Qualifying Free Zone Person (QFZP) pays 0% on its Qualifying Income and 9% on Non-Qualifying Income. The distinction between Qualifying and Non-Qualifying Income is therefore one of the most commercially important questions in UAE tax planning for 2024 and beyond.

Who Can Be a Qualifying Free Zone Person?

A Free Zone Person qualifies as a QFZP if it meets all of the following conditions throughout the tax period:

  1. Maintains adequate substance in the UAE — substance is assessed at the Free Zone level, not just the entity;
  2. Derives Qualifying Income (defined below);
  3. Has not made an election to be subject to the standard 9% CT regime;
  4. Meets the De Minimis threshold: non-qualifying revenue must not exceed the lower of AED 5 million or 5% of total revenue;
  5. Complies with transfer pricing requirements for related-party and connected-party transactions;
  6. Prepares audited financial statements.

Failure to meet any one of these conditions results in the entire entity's income being subject to 9% CT for that tax period.

What is Qualifying Income?

Qualifying Income falls into two broad categories:

1. Income from Transactions with Other Free Zone Persons

Income derived from transactions with other Free Zone Persons is Qualifying Income, provided the income is not attributable to a mainland PE or relates to Excluded Activities.

2. Income from Qualifying Activities with Non-Free Zone Persons

Income from Qualifying Activities conducted with any person (including mainland UAE and foreign counterparties) is Qualifying Income. Qualifying Activities include:

  • Manufacturing of goods or materials;
  • Processing of goods or materials;
  • Holding of shares and other securities (for investment purposes);
  • Ownership, management and operation of ships;
  • Reinsurance services;
  • Fund management services (regulated);
  • Wealth and investment management services (regulated);
  • Headquarters services to related parties;
  • Treasury and financing services to related parties;
  • Financing and leasing of aircraft (regulated);
  • Distribution in or from a Designated Zone;
  • Logistics services.

Excluded Activities: Always Non-Qualifying

The following generate Non-Qualifying Income regardless of who the counterparty is:

  • Transactions with natural persons (unless the activity is a Qualifying Activity);
  • Banking activities (unless regulated);
  • Insurance activities (unless reinsurance or regulated);
  • Finance and leasing activities (unless regulated);
  • Ownership or exploitation of immovable property (other than commercial real estate in a Designated Zone);
  • Intellectual property income (except for QFZPs that also satisfy IP Box conditions — a separate but related analysis).

Adequate Substance: What Does It Actually Mean?

The QFZP must have adequate substance "in the UAE" — not specifically in the free zone, but UAE-wide. Substance is assessed by reference to:

  • Core income-generating activities being conducted in the UAE;
  • Adequate number of qualified employees in the UAE;
  • Adequate operating expenditure incurred in the UAE;
  • Physical premises in the UAE (not just a registered address).

The substance requirement is fact-sensitive. A shell entity with no staff, no physical presence, and management decisions made entirely from abroad will not satisfy substance requirements.

Practical Structuring Considerations

For businesses with mixed Free Zone and mainland activities, a careful analysis of whether to maintain a single entity or a dual structure (Free Zone entity + mainland subsidiary) is essential. The "De Minimis" test means that even a small amount of non-qualifying mainland income can potentially taint the entire Free Zone entity's income — a significant risk for businesses that serve both markets.
